q: and unto Lemnos, land Of stately mansions, sent they Tydeus' son And battle-staunch Odysseus oversea.

s: Lemnos contains Philoctetes (in a rocky cave)
q: They marked the rocky cave where lay the son Of princely Poeas.

s: Lemnos is site of the Lemnian massacre (in the distant past)
q: To vine-clad Lemnos, where in far-off days The wives wreaked murderous vengeance on their lords

s: Achaeans is a Achaean warriors
q: Then at his words each heart and spirit glowed: They donned their armour, and they grasped their shields. Forth of the ships in one huge mass they poured Arrayed with bull-hide bucklers, ashen spears, And gallant-crested helms.

s: Athena sheds Stature and grace
q: For 'twas the glorious Trito-born that shed Stature and grace upon him.

s: Athena causes Philoctetes' wrath (to melt away when he confronts Odysseus and Diomede)
q: But, even as upon that godlike twain He gazed, Athena caused his bitter wrath To melt away.

s: Athena sends breeze (behind the galley sailing from Lemnos)
q: Athena sent a breeze Blowing behind the galley taper-prowed.

s: Podaleirius heals Philoctetes' wound (swiftly, with salves)
q: Swifter than thought he made him whole and sound; For deftly on the wound he spread his salves, Calling on his physician-father's name

s: Agamemnon has tent (wealthy)
q: Then unto wealthy Agamemnon's tent Did all their mightiest men bring Poeas' son

s: Agamemnon offers the gifts to Philoctetes (as amends for abandoning him)
q: With rich gifts will we make amends to thee Hereafter, when we take the stately towers Of Troy: but now receive thou handmaids seven, Fleet steeds two-score, victors in chariot-race, And tripods twelve

s: Achaeans halts Trojan War (until Philoctetes comes to aid the host)
q: Trusting in him, the sons of Atreus stayed Awhile the war

s: Fate governs human lives (determining their sufferings, honours, joys, and woes)
q: and day by day with pitiless hearts Now they afflict men, now again exalt To honour--none knows why; for all the woes And all the joys of men do these devise After their pleasure.

s: Fate are unavoidable human beings (none of earth-born men can shun them)
q: And none of earth-born men can shun the Fates, And of his own will none can choose his way.

s: Philoctetes' wound is caused by venomous water-snake (through an envenomed bite)
q: The festering wound, dealt when the envenomed fangs Tare him of that fell water-snake

s: Philoctetes' wound is incurable wound (before Podaleirius heals it)
q: that fell water-snake, which men Say dealeth ghastly wounds incurable

s: Philoctetes' bow is made by Hercules (with curving horn tips)
q: Lay the great bow, with curving tips of horn, Wrought by the mighty hands of Hercules.

s: Philoctetes' arrows are coated with water-snake venom (deadly venom for hunting and war)
q: With deadly venom of that fell water-snake Were these besmeared.

s: Trojan War is waged against Troy (with the aim of taking its towers)
q: With rich gifts will we make amends to thee Hereafter, when we take the stately towers Of Troy

s: Trojan War depends on Philoctetes (his arrival is necessary for Ilium to fall)
q: it was not foreordained That Ilium should fall until the might Of war-wise Philoctetes came to aid The Achaean host.

s: Philoctetes' recovery is effected by Podaleirius (through healing salves and divine favor)
q: Swifter than thought he made him whole and sound; For deftly on the wound he spread his salves

s: Achaeans sends Odysseus (to Lemnos with Diomede)
q: and unto Lemnos, land Of stately mansions, sent they Tydeus' son And battle-staunch Odysseus oversea.

s: Achaeans sends Diomedes (to Lemnos with Odysseus)
q: and unto Lemnos, land Of stately mansions, sent they Tydeus' son And battle-staunch Odysseus oversea.

s: Ilium is a city (whose fall requires Philoctetes' aid)
q: That Ilium should fall until the might Of war-wise Philoctetes came to aid The Achaean host.

s: Troy is a stately-towered city
q: ere The glorious walls of Ilium stately-towered Be shattered, and her palaces be burned!

s: Troy is a city (Priam's city)
q: No man had carven that celestial form, But Cronos' Son himself had cast it down From heaven to Priam's gold-abounding burg.

s: Paris's death is caused by Philoctetes' wounding of Paris (the wound proves fatal)
q: That day was Paris doomed, for Helen's sake Fighting, by Philoctetes' hands to die.

s: Paris's death occurs on Ida (after Paris leaves Oenone)
q: But Paris, while they talked, gave up the ghost On Ida: never Helen saw him more.

s: Oenone is a Nymph (Paris's former wife)
q: As at the Nymph's feet that pale suppliant fell Faint with the anguish of his wound

s: Oenone is healer of Paris (her hands alone can remove the venom by Fate's decree)
q: His weird Was only by Oenone's hands to escape Death's doom, if so she willed.

s: Oenone refuses to heal Paris (in anger over his abandonment of her)
q: So from her doors she drave that groaning man-- Ah fool! not knowing her own doom, whose weird Was straightway after him to tread the path Of death!

s: Oenone's refusal to heal Paris causes Paris's death (after she drives him away)
q: So from her doors she drave that groaning man-- Ah fool! not knowing her own doom, whose weird Was straightway after him to tread the path Of death!

s: Oenone mourns Paris (with genuine grief after his death)
q: One only heart was pierced with grief unfeigned, Oenone. Not with them of Troy she wailed, But far away within that desolate home Moaning she lay on her lost husband's bed.

s: Philoctetes is a warrior (Poeas' son and renowned archer)
q: Now Poeas' son the while slew Deioneus And Acamas, Antenor's warrior son: Yea, a great host of strong men laid he low.

s: Philoctetes possesses Hercules' arms (given to him by Hercules as his closest friend)
q: All these Hephaestus' cunning hands had wrought For Hercules; and these to Poeas' son, Most near of friends and dear, he gave to bear.

s: Troy has defensive walls long walls (described as imperishable work of the Gods)
q: No strength of theirs Shall breach the long walls, howsoe'er they strive, For in the imperishable work of Gods Weakness is none.

s: Achaeans is a army (besieging Troy)
q: They looked, and saw them come With furious speed against the walls.

s: Achaeans besieges Troy (from outside the walls)
q: Still bide the Danaans here, still gather strength: Now therefore let us man our stately towers, And thence withstand them, fighting night and day

s: Trojans is a army (defending Troy)
q: Now were the Trojans all without the town Of Priam, armour-clad, with battle-cars And chariot-steeds

s: Trojans defends Troy (against the Achaeans)
q: Now therefore let us man our stately towers, And thence withstand them, fighting night and day

s: Trojan War is a armed conflict (between Trojans and Achaeans)
q: Swiftly with helms and shields and spears they stood In close array. The eyes of mighty Zeus From heaven beheld the Trojans armed for fight Against the Danaans

s: Fate determines Paris's death (his doom is fixed before the fatal wound)
q: That day was Paris doomed, for Helen's sake Fighting, by Philoctetes' hands to die.

s: Fate spins her destiny-thread
q: So from her doors she drave that groaning man-- Ah fool! not knowing her own doom, whose weird Was straightway after him to tread the path Of death! So Fate had spun her destiny-thread.

s: Ida is location of Paris's death (Paris dies there after leaving Oenone)
q: But Paris, while they talked, gave up the ghost On Ida: never Helen saw him more.

s: Troy is under siege Achaeans (during the Trojan war)
q: Still bide the Danaans here, still gather strength: Now therefore let us man our stately towers, And thence withstand them, fighting night and day

s: death is a inescapable doom (as represented by Paris's fate)
q: His weird Was only by Oenone's hands to escape Death's doom, if so she willed.

s: Paris is husband of me
q: Husband, to me, to Troy, and to thyself A bitter blow is this thy woeful death!

s: Paris is husband of thy true wife
q: Go, Lie laughing in her arms for bliss! She is better Than thy true wife--is, rumour saith, immortal!

s: Paris is former husband of Oenone (he abandoned her for Helen)
q: O reverenced wife, turn not from me in hate For that I left thee widowed long ago! Not of my will I did it: the strong Fates Dragged me to Helen

s: Paris is wounded by Philoctetes (by poisoned arrows in battle)
q: Then once again the avenger drew the bow, And the barbed shaft of Poeas' son had plunged, Ere he could swerve, 'twixt flank and groin.

s: Paris is consumed by sickness and tormenting thirst
q: his life fainted in him agony-thrilled. As one with sickness and tormenting thirst Consumed, lies parched, with heart quick-shuddering, With liver seething as in flame

s: Paris dies at Ida (after Oenone refuses to heal him)
q: But Paris, while they talked, gave up the ghost On Ida: never Helen saw him more.

s: Oenone is a wife (of Paris (Alexander))
q: Verily evil-hearted Paris was, Who left a leal true wife, and took for bride A wanton, to himself and Troy a curse.

s: Nymphs judge Paris (as evil-hearted and unfaithful)
q: Verily evil-hearted Paris was, Who left a leal true wife, and took for bride A wanton, to himself and Troy a curse.

s: Nymphs judge Oenone (as a virtuous wife who loved Paris more than life)
q: Ah fool, who recked not of the broken heart Of a most virtuous wife, who more than life Loved him who turned from her and loved her not!

s: the pyre is awful
q: Seeking the awful pyre, to leap thereon.

s: the pyre has a great wall of fire
q: Roared up about him a great wall of fire;

s: the pyre contains Oenone (after she leaps onto it)
q: There burned she, clasping Paris.

s: Oenone and Paris's cremation is a cremation
q: But when the blast of the devouring fire Had made twain one, Oenone and Paris, now One little heap of ashes,

s: Oenone and Paris's cremation unites Oenone (in death with Paris)
q: But when the blast of the devouring fire Had made twain one, Oenone and Paris, now One little heap of ashes,

s: Oenone and Paris's cremation unites Paris (in death with Oenone)
q: But when the blast of the devouring fire Had made twain one, Oenone and Paris, now One little heap of ashes,

s: Oenone's death is a death by burning (on the pyre)
q: There burned she, clasping Paris.

s: Oenone is virtuous most virtuous (as judged by the Nymphs)
q: Ah fool, who recked not of the broken heart Of a most virtuous wife, who more than life Loved him who turned from her and loved her not!

s: Oenone loves Paris (more than life)
q: Of a most virtuous wife, who more than life Loved him who turned from her and loved her not!

s: Oenone dies by fire (on the pyre)
q: There burned she, clasping Paris.

s: Paris is a king (of the shepherds' community)
q: For from the mountains far and near had come Shepherds, and heaped the death-bale broad and high For love's and sorrow's latest service done To one of old their comrade and their king.

s: Paris is a comrade (of the shepherds)
q: For from the mountains far and near had come Shepherds, and heaped the death-bale broad and high For love's and sorrow's latest service done To one of old their comrade and their king.

s: Paris is a husband (of Oenone)
q: Verily evil-hearted Paris was, Who left a leal true wife, and took for bride A wanton, to himself and Troy a curse.

s: Paris is evil hearted evil-hearted (as judged by the Nymphs)
q: Verily evil-hearted Paris was, Who left a leal true wife, and took for bride A wanton, to himself and Troy a curse.

s: Paris is a corpse (at the funeral pyre)
q: Through mountain-gorges so she won to where Wailed other Nymphs round Alexander's corpse.

s: Troy is a city (high-built stronghold)
q: Troy's daughters mourned within her walls; might none Go forth to Paris' tomb, for far away From high-built Troy it lay.

s: Neoptolemus is a son of Achilles
q: So them that erewhile on the Danaans pressed Godlike Achilles' son now backward hurled

s: Xanthus is a stream (fair)
q: Whom Lycia nurtured by fair Xanthus' stream

s: Zeus is a Thunderer (husband of Leto)
q: The stream revealed to men by Leto, bride Of Thunderer Zeus

s: Troy is far from Paris' tomb (far away)
q: Paris' tomb, for far away From high-built Troy it lay.

s: Aeneas is a Trojan warrior (son of Anchises)
q: Aye followed on Anchises' warrior son

s: Aeneas is a son of Anchises (warrior of Troy)
q: Aye followed on Anchises' warrior son

s: Aeneas fights Achaeans (alongside Eurymachus)
q: For these against the mighty Achaeans fought Shoulder to shoulder
